terms.label: Algebra
terms.definition:
A unital associative algebra consists of a vector space \(A\), a bilinear multiplication \(m:A\otimes A\to A\), and an element \(1_A\) such that
\[
(ab)c=a(bc),\qquad 1_Aa=a=a1_A.
\]
Equivalently, the unit is a linear map \(u_A:k\to A\), \(u_A(1)=1_A\). For an algebra of operators, associativity is the statement that three successive operations have a well-defined composite.

A left \(A\)-module is a vector space \(M\) together with an action \(\rho_M:A\otimes M\to M\) satisfying
\[
(ab)m=a(bm),\qquad 1_Am=m.
\]
A map of modules \(f:M\to N\) is a linear map with \(f(am)=af(m)\). Such a map compares the systems together with their observable actions, not merely their underlying vector spaces.

For example, let \(A=k[x]\). For every \(\lambda\in k\), there is a one-dimensional module \(k_\lambda\) on which \(x\) acts by multiplication by \(\lambda\). A module map \(f:k_\lambda\to k_\mu\) must satisfy
\[
\lambda f(1)=\mu f(1).
\]
Thus \(k_\lambda\) and \(k_\mu\) are isomorphic precisely when \(\lambda=\mu\). Their dimensions agree for every pair of parameters. A counting invariant of the state space has discarded the action that distinguishes them.

terms.label: Module
terms.definition:
A left \(A\)-module is a vector space \(M\) together with an action \(\rho_M:A\otimes M\to M\) satisfying
\[

\]

terms.label: Coproduct
terms.definition:
Suppose \(M\) and \(N\) are representations of the same algebra \(H\). Their vector-space tensor product exists, but an \(H\)-action on it has not yet been specified. If we have a linear map
\[
\Delta:H\longrightarrow H\otimes H,
\]
we can try
\[
h\cdot(m\otimes n)
=\sum h_{(1)}m\otimes h_{(2)}n,
\qquad
\Delta(h)=\sum h_{(1)}\otimes h_{(2)}.
\tag{2.1}
\]
The notation on the right denotes a finite sum representing the algebraic tensor \(\Delta(h)\).

For (2.1) to be a representation, multiplication must be respected:
\[
\Delta(hh')=\Delta(h)\Delta(h'),\qquad
\Delta(1_H)=1_H\otimes1_H.
\tag{2.2}
\]
For three modules, the two resulting actions agree under the usual vector-space associator if
\[
(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta
=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)\Delta.
\tag{2.3}
\]
This is coassociativity. It compares two maps from \(H\) to \(H^{\otimes3}\).

There is also a distinguished one-dimensional representation if we have an algebra map \(\epsilon:H\to k\). It serves as the tensor unit when
\[
(\epsilon\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta
=\mathrm{id}
=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\epsilon)\Delta.
\tag{2.4}
\]
The map \(\epsilon\) is the **coalgebra counit**. An algebra \(H\) with \(\Delta\) and \(\epsilon\) satisfying (2.2)–(2.4) is a bialgebra.

The product–coproduct compatibility can be written as one equation between maps \(H\otimes H\to H\otimes H\):
\[
\Delta m
=(m\otimes m)
(\mathrm{id}\otimes\tau\otimes\mathrm{id})
(\Delta\otimes\Delta),
\tag{2.5}
\]
where \(\tau(a\otimes b)=b\otimes a\). The middle interchange places the first components together and the second components together. This equation is the ordinary model for one of the compatibility problems in a chiral quantum group. The chiral problem must specify the position-dependent operation spaces and their interchange before it can assert the corresponding equation.

terms.label: Bialgebra
terms.definition:

\]

terms.label: Braiding
terms.definition:
A braiding is a natural family of isomorphisms
\[
\beta_{M,N}:M\otimes N\longrightarrow N\otimes M,
\]
compatible with maps of both input objects. It has its own compatibility with composition. With parentheses identified by the associator, its two hexagon equations read
\[
\beta_{L,M\otimes N}
=(\mathrm{id}_M\otimes\beta_{L,N})
(\beta_{L,M}\otimes\mathrm{id}_N),
\tag{2.9}
\]
\[
\beta_{L\otimes M,N}
=(\beta_{L,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)
(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\beta_{M,N}).
\tag{2.10}
\]
These equations say that moving one object past a pair agrees with moving it past the two factors successively.

For ordinary vector spaces, the flip provides such a braiding. For \(H\)-modules it is action-preserving when the coproduct is cocommutative, meaning \(\tau\Delta=\Delta\). A noncocommutative coproduct requires additional data to obtain an exchange map. In local field theories, the exchange can also depend on positions and continuation paths. The associator and hexagon equations then become part of the comparison to be proved.

Here *coherence* means these specified compatibility equations. For complexes, some equalities are replaced by homotopies, which must satisfy further equations of their own. Retaining an associator without its pentagon, or a binary homotopy without the next compatibility, retains only part of the structure.

terms.label: Associator
terms.definition:
Even when tensor products are associative up to canonical isomorphism, the isomorphisms must agree with one another. For three objects there is an associator
\[
\alpha_{L,M,N}:(L\otimes M)\otimes N
\longrightarrow L\otimes(M\otimes N).
\]
For four objects, the pentagon identity says that the two paths from
\[
((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\otimes P
\quad\text{to}\quad
L\otimes(M\otimes(N\otimes P))
\]
agree. One path uses two associators; the other uses three. This is an equation of maps, not merely an assertion that the initial and final objects are isomorphic.

A braiding is a natural family of isomorphisms
\[
\beta_{M,N}:M\otimes N\longrightarrow N\otimes M,
\]
compatible with maps of both input objects. It has its own compatibility with composition. With parentheses identified by the associator, its two hexagon equations read
\[
\beta_{L,M\otimes N}
=(\mathrm{id}_M\otimes\beta_{L,N})
(\beta_{L,M}\otimes\mathrm{id}_N),
\tag{2.9}
\]
\[
\beta_{L\otimes M,N}
=(\beta_{L,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)
(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\beta_{M,N}).
\tag{2.10}
\]
These equations say that moving one object past a pair agrees with moving it past the two factors successively.

terms.label: Adjunction
terms.definition:
Let \(A\) be another dg algebra and let \(W\) be an \(A\)-\(B\) bimodule. Derived tensor and derived Hom give an adjunction
\[
\Phi=W\otimes_B^{\mathbf L}-:D(B)
\rightleftarrows D(A):
\Psi=\operatorname{RHom}_A(W,-).
\]
Its defining property is the natural equivalence
\[
\operatorname{RHom}_A(\Phi L,M)
\simeq\operatorname{RHom}_B(L,\Psi M).
\]
The **unit** \(\eta_L:L\to\Psi\Phi L\) corresponds to the identity of \(\Phi L\); the **counit** \(\varepsilon_M:\Phi\Psi M\to M\) corresponds to the identity of \(\Psi M\). In degree zero the counit is evaluation. Derived resolutions supply its meaning on complexes. These are adjunction maps, distinct from an algebra unit or a coalgebra counit.

The two triangle identities are
\[
\varepsilon_{\Phi L}\circ\Phi(\eta_L)=1_{\Phi L},
\qquad
\Psi(\varepsilon_M)\circ\eta_{\Psi M}=1_{\Psi M}.
\]
They express compatibility of the two reconstructions. The functor \(\Phi\) is fully faithful precisely when every \(\eta_L\) is an equivalence. The functor \(\Psi\) is fully faithful precisely when every \(\varepsilon_M\) is an equivalence. An equivalence of the two whole categories requires both.

terms.label: Field
terms.definition:
Let \(V\) be a complex vector space of states. A **field** on \(V\) is a series
\[
A(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}A_nz^{-n-1},
\qquad A_n\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V),
\tag{3.1}
\]
such that, for each \(v\in V\), the vector \(A_nv\) vanishes for all sufficiently large \(n\). The bound may depend on \(v\). Consequently \(A(z)v\) belongs to \(V((z))\): it has only finitely many negative powers of \(z\), although it may have infinitely many positive powers. The operators \(A_n\) are the **modes** of the field.

The coefficient notation is arranged so that
\[
A_n v=\operatorname{Res}_{z=0}z^n A(z)v\,dz.
\]
Here the formal residue extracts the coefficient of \(z^{-1}\). No analytic integral is required for this definition. If a particular matrix coefficient is represented by a convergent meromorphic function, the same coefficient is its usual contour residue.

The products \(A(z)B(w)\) and \(B(w)A(z)\) initially have different expansion conventions. Their difference is interpreted as a two-variable formal distribution. Two fields are **local** if there is an integer \(N\geq0\) such that
\[
(z-w)^N[A(z),B(w)]=0.
\tag{3.2}
\]
We are using even, or bosonic, fields; fields with odd parity require the corresponding graded commutator. Equation (3.2) says that multiplying by a sufficiently high power of the collision equation removes the difference between the two expansions. It does not assign a finite product at \(z=w\).

terms.label: Locality
terms.definition:
The products \(A(z)B(w)\) and \(B(w)A(z)\) initially have different expansion conventions. Their difference is interpreted as a two-variable formal distribution. Two fields are **local** if there is an integer \(N\geq0\) such that
\[
(z-w)^N[A(z),B(w)]=0.
\tag{3.2}
\]
We are using even, or bosonic, fields; fields with odd parity require the corresponding graded commutator. Equation (3.2) says that multiplying by a sufficiently high power of the collision equation removes the difference between the two expansions. It does not assign a finite product at \(z=w\).

For example, write \(\iota_{z,w}\) for expansion in nonnegative powers of \(w/z\), and \(\iota_{w,z}\) for expansion in nonnegative powers of \(z/w\). Then
\[
\iota_{z,w}\frac1{(z-w)^2}
=\sum_{r\geq0}(r+1)w^rz^{-r-2},
\qquad
\iota_{w,z}\frac1{(z-w)^2}
=\sum_{r\geq0}(r+1)z^rw^{-r-2}.
\tag{3.3}
\]
These are expansions of the same rational function in two different regions. As formal distributions they are different. Multiplication by \((z-w)^2\) makes both equal to \(1\), so it kills their difference. This is the mechanism behind the locality equation for the current below.

terms.label: Vertex algebra
terms.definition:
A vertex algebra packages a compatible family of fields on one state space. In the even convention used here, its data are a vector space \(V\), a vacuum vector \(\mathbf1\), a translation operator \(T:V\to V\), and a linear assignment
\[
a\longmapsto Y(a,z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_{(n)}z^{-n-1}
\]
of a field to every state \(a\). They satisfy the vacuum and creation identities
\[
Y(\mathbf1,z)=\operatorname{id}_V,
\qquad
Y(a,z)\mathbf1\in a+zV[[z]],
\tag{3.4}
\]
the translation identities
\[
T\mathbf1=0,
\qquad
[T,Y(a,z)]=\partial_zY(a,z)=Y(Ta,z),
\tag{3.5}
\]
and locality for every pair \(Y(a,z),Y(b,w)\). These conditions express the state–field correspondence, the infinitesimal motion of an insertion, and the compatibility of products at distinct positions. They imply
\[
Y(a,z)\mathbf1=e^{zT}a,
\qquad a=a_{(-1)}\mathbf1.
\]
Thus the vacuum connects an operator-valued field with the state it creates. It has not yet supplied a scalar-valued vacuum expectation: that requires a linear functional or pairing in addition.

The singular part of the product is written
\[
Y(a,z)Y(b,w)
\sim\sum_{n\geq0}
\frac{Y(a_{(n)}b,w)}{(z-w)^{n+1}}.
\tag{3.6}
\]
The symbol \(\sim\) means equality of singular parts in the indicated expansion convention. The sum is finite for each pair of states. The regular coefficients also belong to the vertex-algebra structure: in particular, \(a_{(-1)}b\) defines the normally ordered product. Retaining only (3.6) therefore retains less information than the full state–field map.

One can collect the singular coefficients into a polynomial in a formal variable \(\lambda\):
\[
[a_\lambda b]=\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{\lambda^n}{n!}a_{(n)}b.
\tag{3.7}
\]
This **\(\lambda\)-bracket** is convenient for differential identities. It records the singular products; it is not, by itself, a definition of the full vertex algebra. Beilinson and Drinfeld relate vertex algebras to translation-equivariant chiral algebras on the affine line in *Chiral Algebras*, §0.15, and express the state–field operation geometrically in §3.5.

terms.label: Differential module
terms.definition:
The coordinate \(z\) made the mode calculation transparent. To move from a disc to a curve, one needs a way to differentiate sections and to compare their descriptions in different coordinates. The sheaf \(\mathcal D_X\) on a smooth curve \(X\) is the sheaf of algebraic differential operators. On an affine coordinate chart its generators satisfy
\[
[\partial_z,z]=1.
\]
A left **differential module**, or left \(\mathcal D_X\)-module, is an \(\mathcal O_X\)-module \(M\) with differentiation obeying the Leibniz rule
\[
\nabla_{\partial_z}(fm)=f'm+f\nabla_{\partial_z}m.
\tag{3.14}
\]
For a vector bundle this is a connection. Differential modules may also be infinite-dimensional or supported on a subvariety, so they include more than vector bundles with connection.

On the coordinate line, a vector space with an operator \(T\) gives the example \(M=\mathcal O_X\otimes V\) with
\[
\nabla_{\partial_z}(f\otimes v)=f'\otimes v+f\otimes Tv.
\]
The equation records translation together with differentiation of scalar coefficients. It does not, on its own, give the response of a vertex algebra to every nonlinear coordinate change. To obtain a coordinate-independent construction on arbitrary curves, one supplies suitable coordinate-change actions; a conformal structure is a familiar way to obtain them. Translation-equivariant algebras on the affine line and coordinate-independent algebras on all curves are therefore different global assertions.

Chiral operations are conventionally written for right differential modules. If \(M\) is a left module, its corresponding right module is
\[
M^{\mathrm r}=\omega_X\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}M,
\]
where \(\omega_X\) is the line bundle of one-forms. In a coordinate,
\[
(dz\otimes m)\cdot\partial_z=-dz\otimes\nabla_{\partial_z}m.
\tag{3.15}
\]
This conversion accounts for the signs and one-form factors in a geometric residue. It is an equivalence between left and right differential modules; it is not a duality of the state spaces.

terms.label: Configuration space
terms.definition:
Let \(X\) be a smooth algebraic curve over a characteristic-zero field \(k\). For a finite nonempty set \(I\), the product \(X^I\) records an \(I\)-labelled family of points. Its open configuration space is
\[
U_I=\{(x_i)\in X^I:x_i\ne x_j\text{ whenever }i\ne j\}.
\tag{4.1}
\]
Write \(j_I:U_I\hookrightarrow X^I\) for its inclusion. The **small diagonal** is the map
\[
\Delta_I:X\longrightarrow X^I,
\qquad x\longmapsto(x)_{i\in I}.
\]
Its image is the locus where all the labelled points coincide. For two labels \(i,j\), the partial diagonal \(\Delta_{ij}\) imposes only \(x_i=x_j\).

A partition of the labels specifies which points are to be treated as one cluster. Represent it by a surjection \(\pi:J\twoheadrightarrow I\), with blocks \(J_i=\pi^{-1}(i)\). Define
\[
U_\pi=\{(x_j)\in X^J:
x_j\ne x_{j'}\text{ if }\pi(j)\ne\pi(j')\}.
\tag{4.2}
\]
Points in different blocks must be distinct; points in the same block may collide. The associated diagonal map
\[
\Delta_\pi:X^I\longrightarrow X^J,
\qquad(x_i)\longmapsto(x_{\pi(j)})
\]
inserts one repeated coordinate for every label in a block. Its image is the locus where the points in each block coincide.

terms.label: Chiral operation
terms.definition:
The direct image \(\Delta_{I*}M\) is a differential module on \(X^I\) supported on the small diagonal. It includes derivatives in directions normal to that diagonal. A **chiral \(I\)-operation** is a differential-module map
\[
\mu:
j_{I*}j_I^*\Bigl(\boxtimes_{i\in I}L_i\Bigr)
\longrightarrow\Delta_{I*}M.
\tag{4.3}
\]
Thus its space is
\[
P_I^{\mathrm{ch}}((L_i);M)
=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal D_{X^I}}
\left(j_{I*}j_I^*\boxtimes_iL_i,\Delta_{I*}M\right).
\tag{4.4}
\]
Both sides of the Hom belong to the same category on \(X^I\). The source permits separated inputs and their poles; the target records an output concentrated at their collision. This is the operation space of Beilinson–Drinfeld, *Chiral Algebras*, §3.1.1.

The simplest model is a residue. With a local normal coordinate \(t=z-w\), the functional associated to a pole of order \(r\) acts on a test series \(f(t)\) by
\[
\operatorname{Res}_{t=0}\frac{f(t)}{t^r}\,dt
=\frac{f^{(r-1)}(0)}{(r-1)!}.
\tag{4.5}
\]
A simple pole extracts a value; a double pole extracts a first derivative. Higher poles retain higher normal derivatives. The target in (4.3) is designed to hold this information. Substituting \(z=w\) into a singular function would not define the operation.

For three inputs, one can compose a binary operation on the first block with a second binary operation on its output and the remaining input. The partition open \(U_\pi\) keeps distinct clusters apart during the first step. Localization and the diagonal direct-image identities then place the composite in \(P_J^{\mathrm{ch}}\). These composition maps are associative. Beilinson–Drinfeld, §3.1.2, writes them for arbitrary surjections of finite sets; the geometry explains the intermediate domains that a bare expression such as \(\mu(\mu(a,b),c)\) suppresses.

terms.label: Factorization algebra
terms.definition:
In the classical algebraic formulation, a factorization algebra consists of quasi-coherent sheaves \(B_I\) on \(X^I\), together with two kinds of identifications. A surjection \(\pi:J\twoheadrightarrow I\) gives the diagonal identification
\[
\nu_\pi:\Delta_\pi^*B_J\xrightarrow{\sim}B_I
\tag{4.7}
\]
and the factorization identification on the block-separation open
\[
c_\pi:
\left.\boxtimes_{i\in I}B_{J_i}\right|_{U_\pi}
\xrightarrow{\sim}
\left.B_J\right|_{U_\pi}.
\tag{4.8}
\]
The diagonal identifications compose under successive collapses. The factorization identifications compose under refinements of partitions, and these two systems agree when some clusters are collapsed while others remain separated. The sheaves have no nonzero local sections supported on the union of collision diagonals. A unit is a section \(1\in B_{\{1\}}\) whose external product with every local section extends across the two-point diagonal and restricts there to that section. These are the ordinary sheaf conditions of *Chiral Algebras*, §§3.4.2–3.4.4; in derived formulations the pullbacks, equivalences and compatibilities need their derived versions.

For example, taking \(B_I=\mathcal O_{X^I}\) gives the unit factorization algebra. The factorization maps are the evident identifications of functions in separate sets of variables; the unit is the constant function \(1\). More interesting examples retain nontrivial collision data even though their restrictions to pairwise-distinct points are external products.

The full family is often described as a sheaf on the **Ran space** of \(X\). At the level of points, this is the set of finite nonempty subsets of \(X\); repeated labels specify the same subset. The maps \(\Delta_\pi\) express exactly those repetitions. One may use the compatible family \((B_I,\nu_\pi)\) without treating the Ran space as an ordinary finite-dimensional variety.

**Theorem: classical factorization and chiral algebras.** The above category of unital factorization algebras is equivalent to the category of unital Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral algebras on \(X\). The factorization sheaves acquire a canonical differential-module structure, and the corresponding right differential module is \(\omega_X\otimes B_{\{1\}}\).

This is *Chiral Algebras*, Proposition 3.4.7 and Theorem 3.4.9. The forward construction uses factorization to compare sections away from diagonals and then applies the geometric residue operation to obtain (4.3). The inverse construction is controlled by a complex indexed by partitions and their diagonals: its differential combines the chiral operations, and its exactness makes the collision extensions compatible. This partition complex is the Chevalley–Cousin complex of §§3.4.10–3.4.12. The theorem is about the full compatible sheaf data, including collisions and the unit. Giving only (4.8) on a separated open set omits part of its hypothesis.

terms.label: Cochain complex
terms.definition:
A cochain complex is a sequence of vector spaces and linear maps
\[
\cdots\longrightarrow V^{n-1}\xrightarrow{d}V^n
\xrightarrow{d}V^{n+1}\longrightarrow\cdots,
\qquad d^2=0.
\]
The superscript is the **cohomological degree**, and the differential has degree \(+1\). A vector killed by \(d\) is a cycle; a vector of the form \(dw\) is a boundary. Their quotient is
\[
H^n(V)=\ker(d:V^n\to V^{n+1})/
\operatorname{im}(d:V^{n-1}\to V^n).
\]
The distinction between a boundary and a chosen primitive matters. Knowing that \(v=dw\) is solvable does not specify \(w\), and different choices can enter later operations.

Our shift convention is
\[
V[1]^n=V^{n+1},\qquad d_{V[1]}=-d_V.
\]
Thus a vector of degree \(r\) in \(V\) has degree \(r-1\) in \(V[1]\). Write \(sv\) for that shifted vector; \(s\) has degree \(-1\). Tensor products use the Koszul sign rule:
\[
d(v\otimes w)=dv\otimes w+(-1)^{|v|}v\otimes dw,
\]
where \(|v|\) denotes the degree of a homogeneous vector.

A chain map \(f:V\to W\) commutes with the differentials. A homotopy from \(g\) to \(f\) is a degree-minus-one map \(h\) satisfying
\[
f-g=d_Wh+hd_V.
\]
Homotopic maps induce the same cohomology map, but the homotopy contains information that this induced map forgets. More generally, maps of all degrees form a complex
\[
\operatorname{Hom}^r(V,W)=\prod_n\operatorname{Hom}(V^n,W^{n+r}),
\qquad
\partial f=d_Wf-(-1)^rfd_V.
\]
Chain maps are its degree-zero cycles, and homotopies identify maps whose difference is a boundary. The product over \(n\) is intentional: a degree-\(r\) map has a component on every degree of \(V\).

A chain map is a **quasi-isomorphism** if it induces an isomorphism on every cohomology group. The ordinary **derived category** formally makes these maps invertible. We will also retain the derived mapping complexes, obtained by resolving the inputs as necessary, rather than keeping only their degree-zero cohomology. This enhanced form of the derived category remembers homotopies and homotopies between them; it is the meaning intended when the geometric theorem below refers to higher mapping spaces.

terms.label: Massey product
terms.definition:
Changing \(x\) or \(y\) by a degree-one cycle changes \([z]\) by an element of
\([a]H^1(A)+H^1(A)[c]\). In this example \(H^1(A)\) is spanned by \([a],[b],[c]\), and that indeterminacy cannot remove the words \(ay\) and \(xc\). The resulting nonzero coset is a **triple Massey product**: a higher operation defined from two vanishing products and choices of their primitives. The multiplication table on cohomology records the two zero products but does not determine this further class.

terms.label: Bar construction
terms.definition:
An augmentation of a unital dg algebra is a dg algebra map \(\epsilon:A\to k\), where \(k\) is the ground field. It splits the underlying complex as
\(A=k\cdot1\oplus\bar A\), with \(\bar A=\ker\epsilon\). The **reduced bar construction**, including its empty word, is
\[
BA=T^c(\bar A[1])
=k\oplus\bigoplus_{n\ge1}(\bar A[1])^{\otimes n}.
\]
We write
\[
[a_1|\cdots|a_n]=sa_1\otimes\cdots\otimes sa_n,
\qquad
|[a_1|\cdots|a_n]|=\sum_i|a_i|-n.
\]
The superscript \(c\) indicates the tensor **coalgebra**. Its coproduct splits a word at every position:
\[
\Delta[a_1|\cdots|a_n]
=\sum_{i=0}^n[a_1|\cdots|a_i]
\otimes[a_{i+1}|\cdots|a_n].
\]
The empty word is \(1\). This deconcatenation is coassociative because splitting at two positions gives the same three consecutive subwords in either order.

The bar differential has two kinds of terms. It applies the differential of \(A\) to one letter, or multiplies two adjacent letters. With our cohomological suspension convention, its defining components are
\[
b_1(sa)=-s(da),\qquad
b_2(sa\otimes sb)=(-1)^{|a|}s(ab).
\]
They extend to words by applying the operation in each possible position. Passing a degree-one operation across a prefix contributes the degree of that prefix. Explicitly,
\[
\begin{aligned}
b[a_1|\cdots|a_n]
={}&\sum_{i=1}^n
(-1)^{1+\sum_{j<i}(|a_j|-1)}
[a_1|\cdots|da_i|\cdots|a_n]\\
&+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}
(-1)^{|a_i|+\sum_{j<i}(|a_j|-1)}
[a_1|\cdots|a_ia_{i+1}|\cdots|a_n].
\end{aligned}
\]
The equation \(b^2=0\) expresses three familiar facts: \(d^2=0\), the Leibniz rule, and associativity. For an ordinary algebra concentrated in degree zero, the internal-differential terms vanish, and
\[
b[a|b]=[ab],\qquad
b[a|b|c]=[ab|c]-[a|bc].
\]
Applying \(b\) again gives \([(ab)c]-[a(bc)]=0\). The length-three word makes the relation between the two multiplications into an explicit boundary equation. Longer words organize the compatible ways of repeating this operation. These are the usual algebraic bar formulas, expressed in cohomological degrees; see Loday–Vallette, [*Algebraic Operads*, §§2.2–2.3](https://www.math.univ-paris13.fr/~vallette/Operads.html).

terms.label: Coherent associative algebra
terms.definition:
The word complex also accommodates multiplication that is associative only through specified homotopies. A degree-one map \(b\) on \(T^c(V[1])\) is a **coderivation** if
\[
\Delta b=(b\otimes1+1\otimes b)\Delta,
\]
with the graded tensor convention. Such a map is determined by its components
\[
b_n:(V[1])^{\otimes n}\longrightarrow V[1].
\]
On a finite word only finitely many components can act. An uncurved \(A_\infty\)-algebra structure is a coderivation with no constant component and with \(b^2=0\). Undoing the shifts gives operations \(m_n:V^{\otimes n}\to V\) of degree \(2-n\). The suspended formulation fixes the signs without a separate convention for every arity.

terms.label: Conilpotent coalgebra
terms.definition: Let \(C=k\oplus\bar C\) be a coaugmented dg coalgebra. Its reduced coproduct is \(\bar\Delta:\bar C\to\bar C\otimes\bar C\), obtained by removing the two terms involving \(1\). The coalgebra is **conilpotent** if sufficiently many iterated reduced coproducts kill each element. The tensor coalgebra above has this property because a word cannot be split into more nonempty pieces than its length.

terms.label: Cobar construction
terms.definition:
The cobar construction is the tensor algebra
\[
\Omega C=T(\bar C[-1]).
\]
Write \(uc\) for a generator in \(\bar C[-1]\), so \(|uc|=|c|+1\). If \(\bar\Delta c=\sum c'\otimes c''\), its differential is the derivation determined by
\[
d_\Omega(uc)=-u(d_Cc)
+\sum(-1)^{|c'|+1}(uc')(uc'').
\]
Thus bar shortens words by multiplication, while cobar lengthens them by coproduct. The signs are compatible: when \(a,b\) have degree zero, the generator \(u[a|b]\) in \(\Omega BA\) satisfies
\[
d_\Omega u[a|b]=-u[ab]+(u[a])(u[b]).
\]
The map \(\Omega BA\to A\) sending \(u[a]\) to \(a\) and the longer single generators to zero respects this equation. Its extra generators explicitly encode the multiplication relations in \(A\).

More generally, a degree-one map \(\tau:C\to A\), vanishing on the coaugmentation and landing in \(\bar A\), is a **twisting cochain** when
\[
d_A\tau+\tau d_C+\mu_A(\tau\otimes\tau)\bar\Delta=0.
\]
Here \((\tau\otimes\tau)(c'\otimes c'')=(-1)^{|c'|}\tau(c')\otimes\tau(c'')\). This one equation says exactly that \(uc\mapsto\tau(c)\) extends to a dg algebra map \(\Omega C\to A\). For conilpotent \(C\), iterating its reduced coproduct gives the corresponding dg coalgebra map \(C\to BA\). We obtain the strict bar–cobar adjunction
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\rm dgAlg}(\Omega C,A)
\cong\operatorname{Tw}(C,A)
\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\rm dgCoalg}(C,BA).
\]
An adjunction provides comparison maps. Whether those maps are equivalences requires a theorem about the objects and weak equivalences under consideration. The geometry of ordered configurations supplies an especially useful finiteness condition for such a theorem.

terms.label: Twisting cochain
terms.definition:
More generally, a degree-one map \(\tau:C\to A\), vanishing on the coaugmentation and landing in \(\bar A\), is a **twisting cochain** when
\[

\]

For conilpotent \(C\), iterating its reduced coproduct gives the corresponding dg coalgebra map \(C\to BA\). We obtain the strict bar–cobar adjunction

\cong\operatorname{Tw}(C,A)

\]

terms.label: K-flat and K-injective
terms.definition: A right dg module \(P\) is **K-flat** if \(P\otimes_B X\) is acyclic whenever the left dg module \(X\) is acyclic. Such a module computes derived tensor on arbitrary coefficients. Dually, a complex \(J\) is **K-injective** if its Hom complex from every acyclic complex is acyclic. This condition concerns the whole complex; injectivity of each term alone does not suffice in the unbounded case. See the [Stacks Project, §13.31](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/070G).

terms.label: Smooth affine module
terms.definition:
Put
\[
\mathfrak n=t\mathfrak g[t],\qquad
\mathfrak l=\mathfrak g[t^{-1}],\qquad
R=U(\mathfrak g),\qquad H=U(\mathfrak l).
\]
A module is **smooth** if each vector is annihilated by \(t^N\mathfrak g[t]\) for some \(N\), which may depend on the vector. Consider the induced smooth module
\[
W=A_\ell\otimes_{U(\mathfrak n)}\mathbb C.
\]
The Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorem identifies its underlying vector space with \(H\). Its energy-zero part is the regular \(R\)-module. This distinguishes \(W\) from the scalar-top vacuum
\[
V=A_\ell\otimes_{U(\mathfrak g[t])}\mathbb C,
\]
whose energy-zero part is \(\mathbb C\).

terms.label: Raw affine level
terms.definition:
Let \(\mathfrak g\) be a nonzero finite-dimensional simple complex Lie algebra. Choose an invariant form \(\kappa\), normalized so that long roots have squared length two, and write
\[
\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}x\,\operatorname{ad}y)
=h^\vee\kappa(x,y).
\]
The integer \(h^\vee\) is the dual Coxeter number. For a scalar parameter \(k\), set \(\ell=(-k-h^\vee)\kappa\). The affine mode algebra \(A_\ell\) has relations
\[
[xt^r,yt^q]=[x,y]t^{r+q}
+r\delta_{r+q,0}\ell(x,y)1.
\]
The scalar \(-k-h^\vee\) is its **raw affine level**: it is the coefficient of the central cocycle in this normalization. The mode algebra here has no degree derivation. Its internal energy grading assigns energy \(-r\) to \(xt^r\).

terms.label: Localizing subcategory
terms.definition:
Write \(\operatorname{Loc}(W)\) for the smallest full stable subcategory containing \(W\) and closed under arbitrary coproducts and retracts. In the internally graded case use all energy shifts:
\[
\mathscr C=
\begin{cases}
\operatorname{Loc}_{\mathscr S_\ell}(W),&\text{ungraded},\\
\operatorname{Loc}_{\mathscr S_\ell}
\{W\langle r\rangle:r\in\mathbb Z\},&\text{graded}.
\end{cases}
\]
Under the preceding full-unit theorem,
\[
D(B)\simeq\mathscr C.
\tag{6.8}
\]
The source is generated by \(B\), or by all its internal shifts, using semifree resolutions. The left adjoint preserves coproducts and sends these generators to \(W\) and its shifts. Full faithfulness also lifts cones and retracts between image objects. These facts identify the image exactly with \(\mathscr C\).

The original counit, not an independently chosen evaluation, is the **coreflection** into this image:
\[
\Phi\Psi M\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_M}M.
\]
This means that for every \(C\in\mathscr C\), it induces an equivalence on derived maps from \(C\). To prove it, the second triangle identity and the full-unit theorem give
\[
\Psi(\varepsilon_M)=\eta_{\Psi M}^{-1}.
\]
The cone of \(\varepsilon_M\) is therefore killed by \(\Psi\), hence is right-orthogonal to \(\mathscr C\). In particular, (6.8) identifies a specified part of the smooth category; it does not assert that every smooth object lies there.

terms.label: Compact object
terms.definition: An object is compact in a category if maps from it commute with arbitrary coproducts. The free module \(B\) is compact in \(D(B)\), so \(W\) is compact **inside \(\mathscr C\)**, with all shifts included when graded. This is a relative compactness assertion. It makes no claim about mapping from \(W\) into arbitrary families outside \(\mathscr C\). The image, compactness and original-counit statements are proved in the same manuscript, §§4–6.

terms.label: Joint augmentation torsion
terms.definition:
There is another plausible description of the image in (6.8), expressed directly in positive-current modules. To keep its ideal distinct from \(I\subset Y_k\), put
\[
U_+=U(t\mathfrak g[t]),\qquad
\mathfrak a=\ker(U_+\to\mathbb C).
\]
A smooth module is **jointly augmentation-torsion** if every vector \(v\) is killed by one whole power \(\mathfrak a^r\). The exponent may depend on \(v\), but it must work for every element of that ideal power. Let \(\mathcal T\subset\operatorname{Sm}(A_\ell)\) be this torsion category and set
\[
D_{\mathfrak a}=
\{M\in\mathscr S_\ell:H^q(M)\in\mathcal T
\text{ for every }q\}.
\]
The cellular category \(\mathscr C\) generated by \(W\) and its required shifts lies in \(D_{\mathfrak a}\).

Finite augmentation quotients explain a substantial converse. Since \(\mathfrak g\) is simple, \(U_+\) is generated in positive current degree one, and
\[
\mathfrak a^r=\bigoplus_{d\ge r}(U_+)_d.
\]
The quotient \(U_+/\mathfrak a^r\) is finite dimensional. The induced module
\[
E_r=A_\ell\otimes_{U_+}(U_+/\mathfrak a^r)
\]
has a finite filtration with factors
\[
W\langle-j\rangle\otimes_{\mathbb C}(U_+)_j,
\qquad 0\le j<r,
\]
where the last factor is a multiplicity space. Resolutions by such modules show that every complex whose terms are torsion is cellular. Every object with bounded-below torsion cohomology is also cellular. These statements, and the cellular coreflector on the whole unbounded smooth category, are proved in *Augmentation torsion and unbounded affine cellularization*.

terms.label: Centre
terms.definition:
Let \(A\) be a unital associative algebra over a characteristic-zero field \(k\). Its centre is
\[
Z(A)=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for every }a\in A\}.
\]
For every left \(A\)-module \(M\), a central element gives an \(A\)-linear operator \(m\mapsto zm\), naturally in \(M\). Conversely, every natural endomorphism of the identity functor on \(A\)-modules arises this way. Indeed, its value on the regular module is determined by \(z=\eta_A(1)\). Naturality with respect to right multiplication by \(a\) gives \(az=za\); naturality with respect to \(A\to M, b\mapsto bm\), then gives \(\eta_M(m)=zm\).

Thus the same element acts compatibly on every representation. This explains why a centre is relevant to bulk–boundary questions: an operation that can be moved without changing its interaction with boundary observables should produce compatible operators on boundary representations. Additional geometric structure is needed to turn this motivation into a statement about a field theory.

terms.label: Hochschild cochains
terms.definition:
The module interpretation also explains the derived replacement. Write \(A^e=A\otimes_k A^{\mathrm{op}}\). An \(A\)-bimodule map \(A\to A\) is determined by a central element, so
\[
Z(A)=\operatorname{Hom}_{A^e}(A,A).
\]
Replacing Hom by its derived functor gives the Hochschild cochain complex
\[
C^\bullet(A,A)\simeq R\operatorname{Hom}_{A^e}(A,A).
\]
For an ordinary algebra over \(k\), the bar resolution represents this complex by \(C^n(A,A)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(A^{\otimes n},A)\). Its first differentials are
\[
(bz)(a)=az-za,\qquad
(bf)(a_1,a_2)=a_1f(a_2)-f(a_1a_2)+f(a_1)a_2.
\]
Consequently \(HH^0(A)=Z(A)\), while \(HH^1(A)\) consists of derivations modulo inner derivations. Higher degrees retain further compatibility data.

A class represented by a bimodule map \(A\to A[n]\) acts on a derived left module through
\[
M\simeq A\otimes_A^L M
\longrightarrow A[n]\otimes_A^L M\simeq M[n].
\]
Here differentials have degree \(+1\), and \(V[1]^j=V^{j+1}\). The derived centre retains these operations and their coherent compositions. Hochschild cochains carry an \(E_2\)-algebra structure: products are accompanied by homotopies encoding their interchange. On cohomology this includes the cup product and the degree-minus-one Gerstenhaber bracket. An equivalence of underlying complexes alone does not identify those operations. See [Higher Algebra, §5.3.1](https://www.math.ias.edu/~lurie/papers/HA.pdf) and [Gerstenhaber’s construction](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/Ger63.pdf).

terms.label: Actor and pointing
terms.definition:
We call such a coalgebra an **actor** when it parametrizes operations on another object. The word does not add a multiplication to \(F\). Two tensor products occur. Disjoint convolution, written \(\star\), combines configurations by splitting their labels; its unit \(K\) is concentrated at the empty configuration. The tensor \(\otimes^!\) combines two coefficient systems at the same configuration by extraordinary pullback along the diagonal. Its unit \(J\) has the local unit coefficient at each configuration. A pointing is an actual coherent coalgebra map
\[
u:J\longrightarrow F.
\]
It specifies a vacuum operation together with all its compatibility homotopies. It contains more information than a class in the singleton cohomology. These conventions are those of the [ordered-collision coalgebra construction](#ref-ch07-01), particularly its coalgebra category and diagonal tensor.

The smallest useful test algebra has two orthogonal idempotents:
\[
B=kp_1\oplus kp_2,\qquad p_ip_j=\delta_{ij}p_i.
\]
Let \(C=C_B\) be its Chevalley coalgebra: its coefficients are built from finite partitions with a \(B\)-label on each block, and its differential merges blocks using the product of \(B\). It has multiplication \(m:C\otimes^!C\to C\) and total unit pointing \(u_B:J\to C\). The two idempotents distinguish two colours of input and output.

A character of \((F,u)\) is a coalgebra map \(g:F\to C\) together with a specified homotopy \(gu\simeq u_B\). An action is a coalgebra map \(\alpha:F\otimes^!C\to C\) together with a specified homotopy \(\alpha(u\otimes^!1_C)\simeq1_C\). There is no additional associative-action axiom involving a multiplication on \(F\). To retain the specified homotopies and homotopies between them, define the complete spaces
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal X(F,u)
&=\operatorname{hofib}_{u_B}\left[
\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(F,C)
\xrightarrow{u^*}\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(J,C)\right],\\
\mathcal A_C(F,u)
&=\operatorname{hofib}_{1_C}\left[
\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(F\otimes^!C,C)
\xrightarrow{(u\otimes^!1_C)^*}\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(C,C)\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
A homotopy fibre records a point upstairs and a path from its image to the specified base point; its higher simplices record the remaining compatibilities.

terms.label: Homotopy fibre
terms.definition:
A character of \((F,u)\) is a coalgebra map \(g:F\to C\) together with a specified homotopy \(gu\simeq u_B\). An action is a coalgebra map \(\alpha:F\otimes^!C\to C\) together with a specified homotopy \(\alpha(u\otimes^!1_C)\simeq1_C\). There is no additional associative-action axiom involving a multiplication on \(F\). To retain the specified homotopies and homotopies between them, define the complete spaces
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal X(F,u)
&=\operatorname{hofib}_{u_B}\left[
\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(F,C)
\xrightarrow{u^*}\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(J,C)\right],\\
\mathcal A_C(F,u)
&=\operatorname{hofib}_{1_C}\left[
\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(F\otimes^!C,C)
\xrightarrow{(u\otimes^!1_C)^*}\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(C,C)\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
A homotopy fibre records a point upstairs and a path from its image to the specified base point; its higher simplices record the remaining compatibilities.

terms.label: Recognition
terms.definition:
There are explicit maps
\[
\Theta(g)=m(g\otimes^!1_C),\qquad
\Psi(\alpha)=\alpha(1_F\otimes^!u_B).
\]
The first turns a character into an operation by multiplication. The second evaluates an operation on the target vacuum. The unit identity gives \(\Psi\Theta\simeq1\). **Recognition** asks whether \(\Theta\Psi\simeq1\) as well, on the full action space. This requires a coherent reconstruction of the operation, not only agreement on singleton values.

terms.label: Spectator
terms.definition: Adding fixed field insertions to the source produces rational forms with **spectators**: labelled positions \(z_1,\ldots,z_r\) that remain as parameters while auxiliary marked positions \(w_1,\ldots,w_m\) are differentiated or absorbed by residues. Three sets of nonnegative integer bounds control the poles: \(N_{ij}\) for spectator pairs, \(b_j\) for a marked point meeting spectator \(j\), and a positive odd integer \(\mu\) for marked pairs.

terms.label: Coordinatewise tensor completion
terms.definition: Give the image the coordinatewise topology inherited from the full matrix space. Its completion is the full matrix space: finite-support matrices are dense, and the finite diagonal matrices converge coordinatewise to \((\delta_{ij})\). The identity matrix becomes available after this specified completion. Nothing in this calculation identifies the completion with a tensor product defined using a different topology.

terms.label: Laurent series
terms.definition:
For a vector space \(V\) over a field \(F\), define

\[
V((q))=\bigcup_{N\in\mathbb Z}q^N V[[q]].
\]

An element has one lower Laurent bound and an arbitrary sequence of coefficients in \(V\).

terms.label: Relative current complex
terms.definition:
Let \(Z_I\) be the union of physical pair diagonals, where both height and complex position coincide. Write \(\mathcal M_Z\) for currents in \(\mathcal M_I\) supported there. The relative complex is

\[
\mathcal F_{\mathcal M}^n
 =\mathcal M_I^n\oplus\mathcal M_Z^{n+1},
\qquad
d_F(\alpha,\gamma)=(\mathcal D\alpha+\gamma,-\mathcal D\gamma).
\]

terms.label: Normalized boundary hypothesis
terms.definition: Throughout the sewing results below, the **normalized boundary hypothesis** is retained: for algebraic external states, the two four-point inverse-Gram sewings converge in their respective channel discs, their marked channel vectors lie in the canonical spectral \(L^2\) spaces, and the two are related by the specified real unitary fusion transformation. We also retain the normalized positive-label pentagon when comparing trees. These are substantive hypotheses. The role of quantum-group harmonic analysis in constructing fusion transformations is developed by [Ponsot and Teschner, *Liouville bootstrap via harmonic analysis on a noncompact quantum group*](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9911110); analytic continuation of fusion coefficients alone does not supply every completed-source estimate used here.

terms.label: Determinant line
terms.definition:
Their coordinate dependence is organized by the determinant line

\[
\operatorname{Det}C
=\bigotimes_j(\det C^j)^{(-1)^j}.
\]

An exponent \(-1\) means the dual line. The cotangent semidensity line in this construction is \((\operatorname{Det}C)^{-1}\). A semidensity transforms by the square root of the Berezinian, the graded analogue of a Jacobian. For a coefficient change \(A\), the cotangent lift has Berezinian \((\operatorname{Ber}A)^2\), and the transported semidensity acquires \((\operatorname{Ber}A)^{-1}\). The determinant-line description fixes this factor without an independent square-root choice. The continued orientation of the even cycle is retained in a separate flat line. Determinant lines also provide the setting for regularized determinants of elliptic operators; Quillen's construction is a basic example. [Quillen, *Determinants of Cauchy–Riemann operators over a Riemann surface*](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01086022).

terms.label: Normalized state
terms.definition: Here \(\partial_C\) contracts two observable slots with \(C\); the exponential terminates on a polynomial. The unnormalized functional is \(Z(F)=G_C\omega(F)\). Consequently a state is the normalized linear functional \(\omega\), while an amplitude retains the factor and line in which \(G_C\) lives. Positivity is asserted for the actual even probability law when available; odd integration is algebraic Berezin extraction.

terms.label: Cap
terms.definition:
A **cap** is a chosen filling of a boundary together with fields, boundary conditions and normalization that prepare a vector or functional in the specified boundary state space. If an anomaly makes the amplitude line-valued, that line belongs to the data. For a bulk observable \(O\), an exact cap comparison would take the form
\[
Z_M^{\mathrm{bulk}}(O)
=Z_M^{\partial}\bigl(r_M(O)\bigr),
\tag{17.9}
\]
where \(r_M\) is the actual observable comparison and both sides take values in an identified amplitude line. This equation is a target, not a definition of \(Z_M^{\partial}\) by the left-hand side. The state prepared by the filling must be constructed independently, and the comparison must commute with cutting and gluing.

terms.label: Associative chiral algebra
terms.definition: An **associative chiral algebra** in this setting is an augmented associative algebra \(A\) for \(\star\), with positive augmentation ideal, whose bar coalgebra \(BA\) factorizes. Factorization means that its cut coproduct is an equivalence to the external product on each designated separating open set. For word configurations these are consecutive cuts; the ordered collision category also permits ordered decompositions into subsets. The chosen category and cuts are part of the definition. [CQ1]

terms.label: Chiral coproduct
terms.definition:
A compatible **\(E_1\) chiral coproduct** requires further data. Specify a tensor product \(\diamond\) combining systems at the same positions, together with the geometric interchange that makes \(A\diamond A'\) an algebra for \(\star\). A coproduct is then an algebra map
\[
D:A\longrightarrow A\diamond A
\]
with coassociativity and a counit to the \(\diamond\)-unit, or a level-indexed family of such maps. In a derived formulation these include the indicated homotopies and their higher identities. They are not supplied by naming two binary arrows.

The familiar bialgebra identity illustrates the required interchange:
\[
\Delta\mu=(\mu\otimes\mu)
(1\otimes\tau\otimes1)(\Delta\otimes\Delta).
\]
Here \(\tau\) exchanges the middle two factors, and the unit and counit must also be compatible. In chiral geometry the corresponding square uses the actual configuration extensions and same-position tensor. Its arrows must be defined on their pole and support domains. For instance, diagonal tensor of collision coalgebras transports through bar–cobar to
\[
A\diamond A'=\Omega(BA\otimes^!BA').
\]
This construction does not automatically identify \(\diamond\) with a tensor of fields carrying a nontrivial exchange. The latter needs its own comparison. [CQ1, CQ2]

These associative structures should also be distinguished from Francis–Gaitsgory chiral Koszul duality. Their Chevalley chains relate Lie objects and cocommutative coalgebras for the chiral tensor on Ran space. Factorization corresponds to a Lie object supported on the one-point copy of \(X\). Restricting the coalgebra to ordered cuts and then taking associative cobar gives an associative chiral algebra. This uses Lie–commutative Koszul duality as an input; it does not identify it with associative bar–cobar duality, nor construct the additional chiral coproduct. [CQ1, CQ3]

terms.label: Spectral form
terms.definition:
There is a class in which the fields, their exchange, and the tensor product can all be written explicitly. Let \(R\) be a commutative algebra over a characteristic-zero field. Take a flat Hopf algebra \(H\) over \(R\), with bijective antipode \(\mathsf s\), and a derivation and coderivation \(T\) satisfying \(\varepsilon T=0\). Write
\[
\Delta a=a_1\otimes a_2,\qquad a(z)=e^{zT}a,
\]
with summation understood. A **unitary spectral coquasitriangular form** is an \(R\)-bilinear map
\[
\rho_z:H\otimes H\longrightarrow R[z,z^{-1}]
\]
with the following identities:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\rho_z(1,a)&=\varepsilon(a)=\rho_z(a,1),\\
\rho_z(ab,c)&=\rho_z(a,c_1)\rho_z(b,c_2),\\
\rho_z(a,bc)&=\rho_z(a_1,c)\rho_z(a_2,b),\\
\rho_z(a_1,b_1)a_2(z)b_2
&=b_1a_1(z)\rho_z(a_2,b_2),\\
\rho_z(Ta,b)&=\partial_z\rho_z(a,b)=-\rho_z(a,Tb),\\
\rho_z(a_1,b_1)\rho_{-z}(b_2,a_2)
&=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b).
\end{aligned}
\]
The fourth identity specifies exchange, and the last makes exchange reversible. A **level** is a Hopf automorphism \(\eta\) commuting with \(T\) and preserving \(\rho_z\). Choose a group \(\Lambda\) of levels; it need not be commutative. These data define the spectral class of chiral quantum groups considered here. [CQ2]

At level \(\eta\), give \(H\) the right coaction
\[
\delta_\eta(b)=b_2\otimes b_3\mathsf s^{-1}(\eta b_1)
=b_{(0)}\otimes b_{(1)}.
\]
Parenthesized subscripts refer to this coaction, rather than the Hopf coproduct. The field is
\[
Y_\eta(a,z)b
=a_1(z)b_{(0)}\rho_{-z}(b_{(1)},a_2).
\]
One coproduct component creates the translated state; the other contracts with the state already present. Finite coproducts and finite Laurent values of \(\rho\) make this an element of \(H((z))\) for fixed inputs. Denote the resulting field algebra by \(V_\eta\).

**Theorem (spectral field and coproduct construction).** Under the hypotheses above, \(V_\eta\) is a quantum vertex algebra with vacuum \(1\), translation \(T\), and rational exchange
\[
\mathcal S_\eta(z)(a\otimes b)
=a_{(0)}\otimes b_{(0)}\rho_z(a_{(1)},b_{(1)}).
\]
Every finite ordered product on a fixed state has a common finite denominator. For \(V_1=V_{\eta_1}\) and \(V_2=V_{\eta_2}\), their tensor product \(\boxtimes_\rho\) has underlying module \(V_1\otimes_RV_2\) and fields
\[
Y_{12}(a\otimes b,z)(c\otimes d)
=Y_1(a,z)c_{(0)}\otimes Y_2(b_{(0)},z)d\,
\rho_{-z}(c_{(1)},b_{(1)}).
\]
The maps
\[
D_{\eta_1,\eta_2}=(\eta_2\otimes1)\Delta:
V_{\eta_1\eta_2}\longrightarrow
V_{\eta_1}\boxtimes_\rho V_{\eta_2}
\]
preserve fields, vacuum, translation and coaction. They are coassociative, with counit \(\varepsilon:V_{\mathrm{id}}\to R\) at the identity level. They induce maps of residue coalgebras and their augmented associative chiral cobars. Over a field, the same constructions descend to the ordered collision schemes. [CQ2]

terms.label: Contramodule
terms.definition:
A **graded contramodule** is a graded vector space \(Q\) with a degree-zero contraaction \(\gamma:\mathbb T_{B_c}(Q)\to Q\) satisfying
\[
\gamma\eta_Q=1_Q,\qquad
\gamma\mathbb T_{B_c}(\gamma)=\gamma m_Q.
\]
Thus \(\gamma\) evaluates the permitted infinite sums. A **curved differential graded contramodule** additionally has a degree-one connection \(D_Q\) satisfying the Leibniz rule for all these sums and
\[
D_Q(bq)=d(b)q+(-1)^{|b|}bD_Q(q),\qquad D_Q^2(q)=hq.
\]
These objects and their graded contramodule maps form the differential graded category \(\operatorname{CDGContra}(B_c)\), with differential \(f\mapsto D_{Q'}f-(-1)^{|f|}fD_Q\) on maps \(Q\to Q'\). An arbitrary \(Q\) is not assigned a topology: its summations are the contraaction, whereas the specified free objects have the displayed inverse-limit topology.

Writing \(\operatorname{Ch}(\mathcal S_c)\) for complexes in the category of smooth modules, there are actual differential graded adjoint functors
\[
K_c:\operatorname{Ch}(\mathcal S_c)
\rightleftarrows
\operatorname{CDGContra}(B_c):F_c,
\]
The free-on-degree-zero objects with smooth recovered action characterize \(\mathcal S_c\) exactly. For every pair of smooth modules, the iterated-continuous bar complex computes derived Hom and Yoneda composition. The localization making \(K_c,F_c\) inverse on the proposed larger derived categories remains a further problem. [CQ7]

terms.label: Geometric realization
terms.definition:
Set \(\mathcal C_\varnothing=\operatorname{Vect}_{\mathbb C}\). The vacuum at \(I\) is the object actually inserted from the empty set,
\[
v_I=\beta_{\varnothing\to I}(\mathbb C).
\]
A **geometric realization** consists of \(\mathcal O\)-linear functors
\[
F_I:\mathcal C_I\longrightarrow\operatorname{QCoh}(X^I)
\]
and comparisons with the finite-map functors and separated fusion. Here \(\operatorname{QCoh}\) denotes quasi-coherent sheaves. Define the realized vacuum coefficients
\[
B_I=F_I(v_I).
\]
Require their collision and separated-fusion comparisons to be isomorphisms, and require that \(B_I\) have no nonzero local sections supported on the diagonal divisor. Finally, the empty comparison must identify \(B_\varnothing\) with \(\mathbb C\) **as a unital algebra**. An identification of vector spaces alone does not fix the vacuum normalization.

These conditions give a factorization algebra \(B\). Its maps
\[
\Delta_\pi^*B_I\longrightarrow B_J,
\qquad
\left.\boxtimes_j B_{I_j}\right|_U
\longrightarrow B_I|_U
\]
are the images of actual categorical maps. The composition diagrams imply all their finite-set identities. The one-point vacuum is the map \(\mathcal O_X\to B_{\{1\}}\); there is no requirement that \(B_{\{1\}}=\mathcal O_X\).

Beilinson–Drinfeld reconstruction supplies a canonical connection on \(B_{\{1\}}\) with horizontal vacuum. Put
\[
A:=\operatorname{Rec}(\mathcal C,F)
=\omega_X\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}B_{\{1\}},
\]
as a right differential module. Its chiral product is determined by the two-point extension \(B_{\{1,2\}}\). If \(j:X^2\setminus\Delta\hookrightarrow X^2\), the map is the composite
\[
\begin{aligned}
j_*j^*(A\boxtimes A)
&\longrightarrow
\bigl[j_*j^*(\omega_X\boxtimes\omega_X)\bigr]\otimes B_{\{1,2\}}\\
&\xrightarrow{\operatorname{Res}\otimes1}
(\Delta_*\omega_X)\otimes B_{\{1,2\}}
\longrightarrow\Delta_*A.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first arrow uses separated factorization; the last uses the collision comparison. Thus the extension across the diagonal enters the formula itself. For an iterated collision, both orders tensor geometric residues with the same coefficient \(B_I\). The finite-map and partition identities identify the two coefficient maps, so residue substitution gives every chiral operadic identity. On the affine line, translation equivariance gives the corresponding vertex algebra. A conformal vector is preserved when it is included in the input; it is not selected by an abstract tensor category. [GR1, GR2]

terms.label: Ribbon category
terms.definition:
A tensor category records how representations combine, but it need not retain the local fields that act on them. A **ribbon category** also has dual objects, a braiding \(c_{M,N}:M\otimes N\to N\otimes M\), and a natural twist \(\theta_M:M\to M\). The twist is compatible with the braiding and duality:
\[
\theta_{M\otimes N}
=c_{N,M}c_{M,N}(\theta_M\otimes\theta_N),\qquad
\theta_{M^\vee}=(\theta_M)^\vee,
\]
with \(\theta_{\mathbf1}=1\). The braiding satisfies the hexagons, and the evaluation and coevaluation maps satisfy the duality triangles.

Consider a positive-definite even integral lattice \(L\): a finite-rank free abelian group with integral symmetric pairing and \((\alpha,\alpha)\in2\mathbb Z\). Its lattice vertex algebra \(V_L\) is the direct sum of Heisenberg Fock spaces with charges \(\alpha\in L\). The irreducible ordinary modules are indexed by \(L^*/L\), where
\[
L^*=\{x\in L\otimes\mathbb R:(x,L)\subset\mathbb Z\}.
\]
When \(L\) is unimodular, \(L^*=L\), the vacuum is the only simple ordinary module. Its finite semisimple representation category is therefore the ribbon category of finite-dimensional vector spaces, with ordinary exchange and identity twist. The two even unimodular rank-sixteen lattices \(E_8\oplus E_8\) and \(D_{16}^{+}\) give this same category. Their vertex algebras have central charge sixteen and the same torus character, but their weight-one current Lie algebras are different:
\[
\mathfrak e_8\oplus\mathfrak e_8
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathfrak{so}_{32}.
\]
Both have dimension \(496\), and their nondegenerate scalar pairings are isometric over \(\mathbb C\). The state-valued simple pole
\[
J^a(z)J^b(w)\sim
\frac{(a,b)}{(z-w)^2}+\frac{J^{[a,b]}(w)}{z-w}
\]
distinguishes them. Recovering a chiral algebra therefore requires information about how its states extend across collisions. A ribbon category at one point does not contain that information by itself. [GR1]

We will examine three ways to retain it. A category-valued system on configurations has a geometric vacuum whose coefficients reconstruct the chiral algebra. Supported duality compares entire collision complexes, with its reversal of arrows kept explicit. Finite rational categories admit a different reconstruction over a finite-dimensional base algebra. Their successes have different hypotheses, and their comparison is a mathematical question.

terms.label: Pro-object
terms.definition:
Multiplication by the Vandermonde in the auxiliary variables gives an integral coefficient isomorphism
\[
V_n:F^-_{I,n}\xrightarrow{\sim}F^+_{I,n}.
\]
It extends to the full Cousin complexes, their subcomplexes with positive state count at every block, and the corresponding vacuum quotients. Dualizing requires a specified topology. For a perfect right differential-module complex \(P\), use
\[
P^\sharp=\operatorname{RHom}_{D_{X^I/R}}
(P,D_{X^I/R})^t[|I|],
\qquad t(\partial_{z_i})=-\partial_{z_i}.
\]
For an increasing perfect presentation, retain the inverse system of these duals: a **pro-object**. Finite state, pole and normal-derivative data determine a finite stage; no common finite stage for all states is imposed.

terms.label: Brane and BRST differential
terms.definition: The word *open* refers to fields attached to a brane, and *closed* to bulk fields that can couple to them. After choosing a square-zero supersymmetry, both sectors are described by complexes. Gauge symmetry is incorporated by a Becchi–Rouet–Stora–Tyutin, or BRST, differential, with additional ghost variables recording gauge transformations and their relations. The research question is whether an independently defined bulk action can be compared with the boundary's derived operations, including junction composition and higher products. Several exact comparisons below answer parts of this question. Their coefficient rings and fields differ, so the comparison between the physical theories must itself be constructed.

terms.label: Hall correspondence
terms.definition:
Let \(\mathcal M_\alpha\) be a moduli stack of objects of charge \(\alpha\). Here a charge is an additive class, such as a class in a Grothendieck group. Let \(\mathcal E_{\alpha,\beta}\) classify exact sequences with quotient of charge \(\alpha\) and subobject of charge \(\beta\). The two maps are
\[
\mathcal M_\alpha\times\mathcal M_\beta
\xleftarrow{\ p\ }\mathcal E_{\alpha,\beta}
\xrightarrow{\ q\ }\mathcal M_{\alpha+\beta},
\qquad
p(M,B)=(M/B,B),\quad q(M,B)=M.
\]
Pullback along \(p\) places the two inputs on the extension space; pushforward along \(q\) combines all extensions with the same middle object. For constructible functions over \(\mathbb C\), the resulting ordinary Hall product is
\[
(f*g)(M)=\int_{B\subset M}f(M/B)g(B)\,d\chi_c.
\tag{15.1}
\]
The integral is the compactly supported Euler characteristic of the actual subobject varieties, weighted by the constructible function. We use finite charge support and domains on which this integral is defined. The indicator of the zero object is the unit. The order in (15.1) is quotient first, subobject second.

A small counting example explains why subobject geometry matters. In the category of vector spaces over \(\mathbb F_q\), use finite counting in place of Euler integration, and let \(e_1\) be the indicator of a one-dimensional space. Every extension of two one-dimensional vector spaces splits, but
\[
(e_1*e_1)(\mathbb F_q^2)
=\#\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_q)
=\frac{q^2-1}{q-1}=q+1.
\]
The product counts the lines inside the middle object. It does not count just the isomorphism classes of possible middle objects. Over \(\mathbb C\), the constructible-function version gives \(\chi(\mathbb P^1)=2\).

terms.label: Orientation root
terms.definition:
To glue these local coefficient complexes one needs an orientation: a square root of the appropriate determinant line, together with its squaring map. In the determinant convention used here, write
\[
K_F=\det R\operatorname{Hom}(F,F),\qquad
D(F,G)=\det R\operatorname{Hom}(F,G),\qquad
J_F^{\otimes2}\simeq K_F.
\]
An extension requires compatible root maps involving
\(J_F\otimes J_G\otimes D(F,G)\). The cross determinant \(D(F,G)\) is part of the map. Its Euler-characteristic sign is not a replacement for the line itself.

For critical coefficient complexes \(\mathscr P_\alpha\), the extension correspondence must carry an actual morphism
\[
p^*(\mathscr P_\alpha\boxtimes\mathscr P_\beta)
\longrightarrow q^!\mathscr P_{\alpha+\beta}.
\tag{15.2}
\]
Here \(q^!\) is exceptional inverse image, the duality-compatible pullback. By adjunction, (15.2) gives a map after \(q_!\); on a proper middle map this is the usual proper pushforward. The chosen cohomology theory, support convention and degree shifts must make this push-pull operation well defined. Associativity asks that its two composites agree on the actual three-step flag, with the orientation identifications included.

There is a strong orientation theorem on a specific compact domain. Let \(X=S_{\mathrm{Kum}}\times E\), with a Calabi–Yau volume form, and choose a smooth elliptic fibre \(C\subset S_{\mathrm{Kum}}\), points \(p\in C\), \(x\in E\), and \(L\in\operatorname{Pic}^0(E)\). The actual semi-topological components of
\[
A=\mathcal O_C\boxtimes\mathcal O_x,
\qquad B=\mathcal O_p\boxtimes L
\]
generate a subgroup \(\Gamma\cong\mathbb Z^2\). Here a semi-topological component is a connected-component class in the moduli of perfect complexes, with addition induced by direct sum. Deformation in a connected family preserves this class; equality of numerical Chern characters need not identify component classes. On the union of these components, the compact orientation root admits unital associative root maps for every finite ordered flag, without changing its square. The two isomorphism classes of enhancements form an \(H^2(\Gamma,\mathbb F_2)\)-torsor. [Strong orientation on compact two-charge components][strong-orientation]

terms.definition:

terms.label: Rigidification
terms.definition:
Rigidifying the residual central \(\mu_n\) and dividing by the translation subgroup \(E[n]\) defines
\[
\mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{amb}}
=\bigl[(\mathfrak V_n\mathbin{/\mkern-6mu/}\mu_n)/E[n]\bigr].
\]
Here \(\mu_n\) is the group of \(n\)th roots of unity and \(E[n]\) the \(n\)-torsion subgroup of \(E\). The derived stack \(\mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{amb}}\) has a closed nondegenerate \((-1)\)-shifted symplectic form and smooth classical truncation
\[
\mathcal B_n=[(C_n\mathbin{/\mkern-6mu/}\mathbb G_m)/E].
\]
The double slash denotes rigidification: locally the objects are retained while their central scalar automorphism subgroup is quotiented out. The corresponding lifting gerbe is the stack of local choices of a lift, with their scalar automorphisms; it is not just a set of choices. The cyclic formal neighbourhoods of \(\mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{amb}}\) agree with those of \(T^*[-1]\mathcal B_n\). A global algebraic equivalence is known at length one; formal agreement at general length does not assert a global equivalence. Nevertheless, the canonical roots \(K_{\mathcal B_n}\) identify the critical coefficients with \(\mathscr P_n=\mathbb Q_{\mathcal B_n}[0]\). On the common-lifting classical flag stack the resulting map \(p^*(\mathscr P_a\boxtimes_{BE}\mathscr P_b)\to q^!\mathscr P_{a+b}\) is an isomorphism with zero source shift; \(BE\) is the classifying stack of elliptic-curve torsors. These give actual classical Hall arrows at every positive length, compatible with the full ordered flags. [Elliptic Weyl transport, ambient paired reduction and critical coefficients][spherical-reduction]

terms.label: Stable pair
terms.definition: A stable pair on \(X=S\times E\) is a morphism \(\mathcal O_X\to F\) with \(F\) pure of dimension one and zero-dimensional cokernel. Purity means that \(F\) has no nonzero zero-dimensional subsheaf. Reduced Donaldson–Thomas/stable-pair comparison gives a common rational function \(R_{h,d}(v)\), whose Laurent expansion at \(v=0\) is their series for a primitive effective K3 class \(\beta_h\) with \(\beta_h^2=2h-2\).

terms.label: Weil functional
terms.definition:
Use logarithmic scale \(u=\log x\), so multiplication of positive scales becomes addition. For a test \(f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)\), set
\[
\widehat f(z)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(u)e^{izu}\,du,
\qquad
H_f(s)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(u)e^{(s-1/2)u}\,du
=\widehat f(-i(s-1/2)).
\]
Convolution and involution are
\[
(f*g)(u)=\int f(t)g(u-t)\,dt,
\qquad f^*(u)=\overline{f(-u)}.
\]
The complete Weil functional, in this normalization, is
\[
\begin{aligned}
W(f)={}&H_f(0)+H_f(1)-f(0)\log\pi\\
&+\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}\widehat f(r)
\operatorname{Re}\psi(1/4+ir/2)\,dr\\
&-\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{\sqrt n}
\bigl(f(\log n)+f(-\log n)\bigr),
\end{aligned}
\tag{16.1}
\]
where \(\psi=\Gamma'/\Gamma\), \(\Lambda(p^k)=\log p\), and \(\Lambda(n)=0\) otherwise. The first two terms are the polar contributions, the integral is the real-place contribution, and the last sum contains both orientations of every prime power. For instance, the term at \(n=4\) has coefficient \(\log2/2\); it is not a second copy of the prime-\(2\) term. [The test algebra and its scalar functional][trace-foundations]

The completed zeta function
\[
\xi(s)=\tfrac12s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)
\]
is entire. Let \(\rho\) run through its zeros, with multiplicity \(m_\rho\), and write \(w_\rho=-i(\rho-1/2)\). The explicit formula identifies (16.1) with
\[
W(f)=\sum_\rho m_\rho\widehat f(w_\rho).
\tag{16.2}
\]
The decay of the transform and the zero-counting bound give convergence on the stated test class. Formula (16.1), however, can be defined without knowing any zero individually. This distinction is the starting point for a geometric trace construction.

Positivity concerns the quadratic form
\[
Q(g)=W(g*g^*).
\tag{16.3}
\]
Since \(\widehat{g*g^*}(z)=\widehat g(z)\overline{\widehat g(\bar z)}\), a real \(w_\rho\) contributes \(m_\rho|\widehat g(w_\rho)|^2\). A nonreal point does not contribute an absolute square. The Weil positivity criterion equates \(Q(g)\ge0\) for every compact smooth complex test with the Riemann hypothesis. Thus the all-test quantifier is part of the mathematical problem, not a harmless extension of a finite calculation.

terms.definition:

terms.label: Frobenius lift
terms.definition:
Integral arithmetic has an analogous loss of information under scalar evaluation. Fix a prime \(p\), including two. A delta structure is encoded by a Frobenius lift \(\varphi\) through
\(\delta(x)=(\varphi(x)-x^p)/p\). On \(\mathbb Z_p\), take \(\varphi=\mathrm{id}\). At positive finite height \(h\ge1\), put
\[
A_h=\mathbb Z_p[x_0,\ldots,x_{h-1}],\quad
R_h=\varprojlim_nA_h/p^n,\quad
I_h=(p,x_i^p-x_i:i<h),\quad
B_h=\varprojlim_nA_h/I_h^n.
\]
The last ring is the formal completion along the finite-field rational locus, defined independently of any comparison image. For each \(c\in\mathbb F_p^h\), choose the integer representatives \(0\le c_i<p\) in \(\mathbb Z_p\). With these lifts, Chinese remainders give
\[
B_h\simeq\prod_{c\in\mathbb F_p^h}\mathbb Z_p[[z_0,\ldots,z_{h-1}]],
\qquad x_i=c_i+z_i.
\tag{16.13}
\]
The natural \(j_h:R_h\to B_h\) is injective, also modulo every \(p^n\): translation by \(c\) is a polynomial automorphism, and polynomials inject into formal power series over the finite coefficient ring.

Frobenius has the variance
\[
\varphi_h:R_h\longrightarrow R_{h+1},
\qquad x_i\longmapsto x_i^p+px_{i+1}.
\]
It raises height. Its extension to \(B_h\to B_{h+1}\) commutes with \(j\). At the arithmetic point \(a\), evaluate \(x_i\) at \(\delta^i(a)\). This evaluation commutes with Frobenius because \((\delta^i a)^p+p\delta^{i+1}a=\delta^ia\); it does not preserve all normal operations.

To define the normal operation, let \(S_i(x,y)\) be the integral arithmetic addition polynomials, characterized by the free-jet identity \(S_i(x,y)=\delta^i(x_0+y_0)\). The first two are
\[
S_0=x_0+y_0,\qquad
S_1=x_1+y_1-
\frac{(x_0+y_0)^p-x_0^p-y_0^p}{p}.
\]
The quotient polynomial is integral. Use independent divided-power parameters \(t_i\); their symbols \(t_i^{[n]}\) satisfy \(t_i^{[r]}t_i^{[s]}=\binom{r+s}{r}t_i^{[r+s]}\), so the construction does not invert factorials in \(\mathbb Z_p\). Congruence translation is the coaction
\[
\alpha(x_i)=S_i(x,pt).
\]
It extends continuously to the rational-locus completion because it preserves its defining ideal. Extracting the coefficient of \(t_0^{[1]}\) defines the first normal derivation \(D_0\). For \(h\ge2\), in the first two coordinates,
\[
D_0x_0=p,\qquad D_0x_1=-px_0^{p-1}.
\]
The point relation \(h_0=x_0^p+px_1-x_0\) therefore obeys
\[
\operatorname{ev}_a(h_0)=0,
\qquad D_0h_0=p^2x_0^{p-1}-p^2x_0^{p-1}-p=-p.
\tag{16.14}
\]
Modulo \(p^2\), the last coefficient is nonzero. Any comparison factoring through scalar point values would erase an operation that (16.13) retains.

terms.label: Proper trace ideal
terms.definition:
The identity on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is not trace class. One should therefore expect a proper trace ideal, rather than a finite trace on every bounded operator. For \(\mathscr C_s=[V\to U]\), put
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathfrak I^0&=\{(T^{-1},T^0)\in\mathfrak S_1(V)\oplus\mathfrak S_1(U):
dT^{-1}=T^0d\},\\
\mathfrak I^{-1}&=\mathfrak S_1(U,V).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(\mathfrak S_1\) denotes trace-class operators. Composition and \(\delta\) make \(\mathfrak I\) a complete proper nonunital differential ideal of the bounded chain endomorphisms. Its closed graded trace is
\[
\tau(T)=\operatorname{Tr}_UT^0-\operatorname{Tr}_VT^{-1},
\qquad \tau(\delta K)=0.
\]
The last identity follows from \(\operatorname{Tr}(dK)=\operatorname{Tr}(Kd)\). Orthogonal splitting of the closed range of \(d\) contracts this ideal onto \(\mathfrak S_1(K_s)\) by a split differential-algebra quasi-isomorphism. The chain-map equation involves \(d\), whereas taking ordinary Hilbert adjoints involves \(d^*\); a positive differential-star structure does not follow. [Trace-class coefficient homotopies][trace-operations]

The trace-class representatives multiply up to an actual trace-class homotopy:
\[
\Lambda_f\Lambda_g-\Lambda_{f*g}=\delta K(f,g).
\tag{16.9}
\]
The homotopy is obtained by applying the bounded inverse of \(d\) on its closed range to the degree-zero defect. It also satisfies
\[
\Lambda_fK(g,h)-K(f,g)\Lambda_h
+K(f,g*h)-K(f*g,h)=0.
\tag{16.10}
\]
Products of two degree-minus-one homotopies vanish. Equations (16.9)–(16.10), with their mixed-degree versions, assemble into a coalgebra chain map on the bar construction. On a word, it sums over partitions into consecutive blocks of size one or two, applying \(\Lambda\) to a singleton and \(K\) to a pair. The triple identity is exactly the equality needed when a bar differential joins adjacent entries.

This also has an analytic completion theorem. Using the arithmetic ideal \(\mathcal J_a\) defined above, form the coefficient complex \(\mathcal E=[\mathcal J_a\to\mathcal A_a]\) in degrees \(-1,0\). Its degree-zero multiplication and action on \(\mathcal J_a\) are convolution; products of two degree-minus-one terms are zero. On tensor words use the completed projective seminorms
\[
P_{R,N}(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}R^nq_{N,\pi}(x_n),\qquad R>0,
\]
where \(q_N\) is the sum of the two coefficient seminorms. In this nonfactorial entire completion, the bar map is continuous with radius bound
\[
P_R^{\mathfrak I}(Gx)\le P_{C_1R+\sqrt{C_2R},4}(x).
\]
The estimate counts the same singleton/pair partitions. It extends the actual identities, not just a scalar trace, through the specified completion.

Locality asks for different structure. A supported coefficient can carry derivatives normal to a collision locus; a derived diagonal product also retains the classes measuring nontransverse intersection. Supported mapping complexes, such normal-jet sheaves, Gaussian preparation and completed finite-word comparisons are available. Their linking construction supplies a cyclic vector and nonlocal creation fields. It does not turn the linking algebra into a local field algebra.

terms.label: Interface
terms.definition: The ordinary algebraic model is useful because all its arrows can be written. Let \(A,B\) be differential graded algebras and let \(P\) be an \(A\)-\(B\) bimodule. The two actions commute with the differential. A vector in \(P\) can therefore be acted on by \(A\) from the left and by \(B\) from the right, as an interface can be acted on from its two sides.

introduction:
A boundary of a quantum field theory supports measurements of its own. Local fields can be inserted at different points, combined while separated, and brought together through singular limits. Line operators can meet the boundary or connect boundary conditions. The question of holographic reconstruction is how much of the independently defined bulk theory these boundary observables and their operations determine.

This work develops that question through associative chiral algebras: local products that vary holomorphically with position and retain their associativity together with the required higher compatibilities. A coproduct supplies the action on a combined system from the actions on its factors. Bar constructions organize products and their relations; module adjunctions compare representations through an actual unit and counit; centres formulate the operations that act compatibly on those representations. Configuration geometry and analytic domains specify where these constructions can be composed.

There are substantial reconstruction theorems on precise domains. Connected ordered bar and cobar give an equivalence without a cohomological boundedness restriction. Under the specified smooth realization hypotheses, nonrational affine examples reconstruct every ordinary unbounded line module and identify its exact image. Spectral quantum groups have compatible fields and level-dependent coproducts. Ordinary geometric coefficient systems recover their original chiral algebra. Current operations, analytic sewings, numerical Gaussian states, Hall correspondences and arithmetic traces provide further independently defined constructions, each with its stated hypotheses.

The remaining comparisons ask whether these structures reproduce the prescribed physical products, interfaces, bulk actions and states. An equivalence of underlying complexes need not preserve a product; a separated comparison need not extend across a collision; a full trace need not determine a state algebra; a normalized state need not determine its amplitude line or the state prepared by a geometric filling. The chapters develop the actual maps and their strongest known scopes before stating the exact open questions. The atlas provides a second route to the same mathematical constructions and sources.
